Alor ANNUAL REPORT. 


BOARD OF DIRECTORS. 


This Association has now entered upon the third era of its 
history. It has the honor of being the pioneer organization on 
the continent of America. In 1872 the building on Victoria 
Square was dedicated. That was, indeed, a great effort, and 
considered to be sufficient for the work in this city for all time 
to come. In January, 1892, we entered the present new build- 
ing, which will be the central one in this city, and from which 
branches in the suburbs will follow. In securing this result the 
desire of many years has been realized, and the Association finds 
itself in possession of a building which is second to none on the 
continent, for interior arrangements and adaptation to the special 
work for young men. 

A resumé of the events leading up to this point will not be 
inappropriate :— 

In the year 1886 the Board of Directors decided upon taking 
steps to secure a site for a future Association building in the 
western part of the city. Five prominent sites were carefully 
considered and prices secured. Finally, in January, 1888, the 
present site on Dominion Square was purchased. In May, 1888, 
the Building Committee was appointed, composed of the 
following gentlemen: Warden King, George Hague, Abner 
Kingman, D. W. Ross, L. H. Packard, Wm. Tees, John Kennedy, 
David Yuile, R. H. Holland, J. Murray Smith, Dr. F. W. Kelley, 
D. Bentley, Chas. Cushing, and C. T. Williams. There have 
since been added Henry Birks and James Wilson. The 
following gentlemen have acted as chairmen: Messrs. Warden 
King, John Kennedy, D. W. Ross, and David Yuile, and itis a 


8 


pleasant fact to record that the Committee has remained intact 
until the completion of the work. To these chairmen especially, 
as also to the members of this Building Committee, the Associa- 
tion is placed under an obligation which it does not, and, perhaps, 
will never, fully realize. We record, with great thankfulness to 
God, that the work has been completed with pérfect harmony 
among the members of the Committee, and also with acknow- 
ledged spiritual blessings received in the carrying out of the work. 


A FOURFOLD WORK. 


The Association now aims to help the whole man through its 
fourfold lines of work, viz., the spiritual, mental, physical, and 
social. It is furnished with equipment which will enable it to do 
this work effectively. The reports which follow will only cover a 
period of four months, from January to April 30th. The work 
of the preceding eight months was confined to the daily office 
routine, and the Young Men’s Meeting and Bible Classes, 
which, we are thankful to say, were never discontinued during 
the period of moving. 

AGENCY. 

The agency which it employs is sen, four of whom devote 
their entire time, and 165 render volunteer service. The aim of 
the management will always be to increase volunteer service as 
rendered by the young men. Larger results can be secured 
thereby, and the experience which members gain in definite 
forms of Christian work fits them for greater usefulness in the 
Church as well as in business life. 


CONSTITUENCY. 


Young men come to the Association from the country, from 
across the water, and from city homes. The first need is a 
boarding-house, and the register at the Association is consulted 
by an average of fifty-six young men per month. 

The young man next needs employment, and one of the 
secretaries devotes from ten to twelve o’clock daily in counselling 
with applicants and giving them letters of introduction to 
business houses. There have been 433 applications received 
and 103 situations secured. 


9 


MEMBERSHIP. 


The total membership on April 30th was 1,562. We should 
aim for a membership of 2,000. 


PHYSICAL. 


The young man from the country has been accustomed to 
physical exercise, and the young man from the city has not been 
so favored as to secure that development which is needed to 
meet the requirements of a busy city life. To each of these 
young men the Association offers opportunities for physical 
development which are the best that can be secured in the 
city. The physical department is under the direction of a 
competent instructor, who, after careful physical examination, 
is able to prescribe for each man that form of exercise best 
calculated to correct present defects and give him a sound 
and vigorous body. - The number of members who have 
received examination since the opening is 690. The Physical 
Director is not only master of his special work in the gymnasium, 
but also experienced in outdoor athletics, which enables the 
Association to carry on the work of this department throughout 
the entire year. He is also an active Christian worker, and one 
whose personal influence upon the large class of young men 
under his control must produce the very best results. 


EDUCATIONAL. 


A large number of young men on entering business life in the 
city discover that they have not taken advantage of their early 
educational privileges, and, on this account, fail to secure 
promotion in business. Mental training is a necessity for 
advancement. To meet this, evening educational classes in the 
following branches have been conducted: French, Phonography, 
Commercial Arithmetic, Bookkeeping, Mechanical Drawing, 
Elocution, Chatauqua Literary Society, Vocal Music, and 
Orchestra. Notwithstanding the broken season, 238 young men 
entered these classes, and many were enthusiastic as to the 
practical results secured. Next season’s prospectus is now well 
matured and almost ready for publication, so that we hope to 


10 


have a large “EVENING” COLLEGE for DAY WORKERS, with 
an entrance roll of from four to five hundred of our members. 
The Association offers to its members a reading-room, which is 
well lighted and furnished, and its tables are filled with the 
choicest magazines and periodicals. The library, however, is 
the weak point in this department. It contains only three 
thousand volumes, when there is accommodation for at least 
ten thousand. This will, doubtless, soon be remedied, as the 
Directors confidently hope that some citizen will donate a fund 
for this special work. To supply and wisely direct the reading 
and mental training of young men, is to lay the foundation for 
a strong, healthy manhood, and a useful life. 


SOCIAL. 

Every young man, whether in the boarding-house or in a city 
home, must have the company of other young men. The 
manner in which he spends his evenings will largely determine 
his character. The social side of a young man’s life is the open 
side to temptations, and the one, alas, through which thousands 
of our young men are ruined for time and eternity. The 
Association should, therefore, be the brightest spot in the city, 
and, while it can never be a substitute for the home, it should 
have so much of the home spirit as to make it a point to which 
young men will naturally gravitate. This is pre-eminently true 
of our new building. Its social features, so far as the reception- 
room and parlors, with their open grates, games, illustrated 
books and music, are all that could be desired. Here the 
Keception Committee has done excellent service, but each 
member should consider it his duty to welcome the stranger and 
make him forget his loneliness. Let the Association be the 
meeting place for your appointments, and make it a rendezvous 
for a daily call. See that every young man of your acquaint- 
ance is introduced to your Association and its secretaries. The 
building itself has been the social attraction to our members 
hitherto, and it was not possible, or, perhaps, necessary, to arrange 
definite social meetings. Beginning with September, these will 
be held monthly during next season, and may be looked for as. 
a special feature. 


it 


RELIGIOUS. 


The Association only exists decause it cares for the SPIRITUAL 
NEEDS of young men. It is because the Directors believe that 
young men can be reached and influenced by their fellows 
toward the acceptation of Jesus Christ as their Saviour, that 
they have given time and money and effort to place the building 
asa shining light in the midst of a city’s temptations. To 
neglect the religious work, therefore, would be to be recreant to 
its highest purpose and obligations. The following meetings 
are held weekly for young men: Two evangelistic meetings, 
two Bible Classes for the study of the Scriptures, and three 
training classes for instruction in methods of Christian work. 
Enquirers are met with at the close of these meetings, and their 
names and addresses sent regularly to the Pastors of the 
Churches they attend. It is impossible to record the letters 
written or the personal counsel given by the secretaries concern- 
ing spiritual things, and this department is, perhaps, the greatest 
work which the Association does. We are glad to report that, 
by correspondence, as also by personal interview, it is looked 
upon as a centre in the city for council in these matters, and the 
secretaries trust that every member will feel free to command 
their time in discussing his personal difficulties or discourage- 
ments. The large addition of members presents a field ripe for 
the harvest, and the responsibilities of the workers are, therefore, 
greatly increased. The present need is a larger number of 
consecrated young men who are willing to serve their fellows 
for Christ’s sake. A plan of personal work has been started, 
by which any member can volunteer to take personal thought 
and effort on behalf of some other young man, seeking, as 
Andrew did, to win his fellow to Christ. Although recently 
started, this is already bringing forth good results. 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


We have now the very best facilities to carry on the work of 
this department. They are fully appreciated by a membership 
of 336. The separate Reading Room and Library and Social 
rooms are great attractions. The rooms are closed at six o’clock, 


12 


except on two evenings of each week ; Tuesday evening for the 
working boys, and Friday evening for the regular prayer 
meeting. It was not considered advisable to encourage Juniors 
under sixteen to be out at night. Under the careful supervision 
of Mr. Corbett, who is specially gifted in working amongst the 
boys, there is now being organized a full set of Committees. 
In these, the boys are being trained for present and future 
service. The conversions constantly reported are most en- 
couraging, and the large number who are now interested in 
Training Class work give the brightest promise for the future. 
Through this department the Association is brought in touch 
with the citizens as never before, and, under wise management, 
it must produce the best results, directly upon the boys, and 
indirectly in securing the intelligent sympathy of the parents 
with the Association. 
EXTENSION. 

This is a new branch. The need is to extend this work 
amongst young men, at home and abroad, who are less favored. 
The agencies are the International and Provincial Committees. 
Besides the direct financial help, the object is the education of 
members in SYSTEMATIC GIVING. This is, perhaps, the most 
important result which can be gained. Last year, through forty- 
five members giving from 2c. to 25c. per week, $162.40 was 
contributed. Many a young man who gives nothing to this 
work would be willing, no doubt, to support a man alone in 
some one of these fields, if he were able to do so. Hereisa 
chance for him, as well as others, to unite their gifts, no matter 
how small, with the gifts of others, and accomplish the same 
thing. 

DEATHS. 

During the year we regret to report the loss by death of the 
following members: William Clare, James G. Taylor, Charles 
J. Tuggey, W. C. Davidson, Dr. J. Dugdale, James Coates, and 
George Blair. 

During the year one of our members, the late James G. 
Taylor, left us a legacy of $500. 


13 


NEEDS. 


Having now secured the Central Building, through the 
liberality of the citizens and members, the future policy of the 
Association will be to lay the foundation for permanent results 
on the lines indicated. There are, however, some immediate 
and pressing requirements for the proper prosecution of the 
work in this city. We take the liberty of enumerating them in 
the order of their importance to us, so that our friends and the 
citizens who can help may keep these needs in view when 
considering their “ benefactions,” or drawing up their “ wills.” 


1st. The liquidation of the floating debt on the building of 
about $10,000 to $12,000. 
2nd. The purchase for the Association of a lot of land on 
the water front, say at Point St. Charles, large 
enough for football, lacrosse, and other games, as 
well as boating. 
3rd. 10,000 volumes for the library (at present only 3,000). 
4th. Funds fora Lot and Branch Building at Point ak 
Charles. 
sth. Funds fora Lot and Branch Building at the North- 
East End. : 
For the privilege of service, and for all the young men who 
have been in any way shielded from evil, and especially for 
those whose lives have been turned to follow Jesus Christ as 
their Lord and Master, we desire to thank our God, and do 
most humbly and heartily ascribe all the glory to Him. 


Secretary. 


14 


NEW BUILDING. 


The Building was opened January rst, 1892. During the year, many anxious 
questions have arisen. The Committee has patiently striven to deal with them one by 
one in the best interests of the work, and they desire to record God’s blessing in 
answer to united prayer. They are able to report with great pleasure that satisfactory 
leases have been made for all that portion of the Building which has been set aside 
for rental, making the present revenue from rental over $5,000 per annum. 

The Committee specially desire to thank the ladies of the various churches who 
have so kindly and generously assisted in furnishing the Building, and also those who 
have contributed pictures and other supplies. They cannot present a complete 
statement of the Building, as there are yet. accounts unpaid and subscriptions to be 
received. So soon as these are closed, a complete statement will be presented to the 
Association. Thestatement of the receipts and disbursements for the year is added :—

DAVID YUILE, 


Chatrman. 


FINANCE. 


This Committee has held fifteen meetings. The subscriptions for the year show 
an increase of $399.60 over last year. This is due to the faithful work of the Com- 
mittee, who have given much time and patient effort to the collections. In order to 
meet the expenses of the larger work in the coming year, your Committee would 
suggest that it be enlarged to double its present size. 


15 


We desire to thank the members and citizens for the cheerful manner in which 
the funds are given. It is gratifying to them to know that their money is being well 
gnvested, as can be seen if those who contribute will inspect our new building and 
see the large number of young men who are making use of the privileges. Occasion- 
ally the question is asked, ‘‘ Why is not the Association self-supporting ?” Because the 
privileges offered to each member cost, with careful economy, at least three times the 
amount of his dues. This marks the benevolence of the enterprise, and is the ground 
of its appeal to the citizens for its support. The thanks of the Committee are due to 
Mr. A. G. Olive for his supervision of the books. 

WARDEN KING, 
Chairman. 
AUDITOR’S REPORT. 


MONTREAL, 18th May, 1892. 

To the President and Directors of the Young Men’s Christian Assoctation : 

GENTLEMEN,—We beg to report that we have audited the Books of Account of 
your Association and the statements prepared therefrom for the past year, and have 
certified as to their being correct statements from the said books. 

We have verified the transactions as fully as possible from the documentary 
evidences produced, and are satisfied that the revenues have been fully accounted for. 

Yours respectfully, 
P..‘5;, ROSS. & SONS, 


Accountants.

MEMBERSHIP. 


Your Committee beg to submit the following as the present condition of our 
membership :— 


SENIOR—Active...... WN hrs staan be ktie ws OTS 
Associate .....- EL Ie cv finaly ve 553 
—— 1226 
JUNIOR—ACTtIVE .. 6 cee cece eee ee tee eees : 
Associate ..... Hehe OPENS 336 pe hey 
HOUGRARY sus Side’ hewe ts ae dine x away be —76 * 
Total membership...... ay 1,638 


In comparison with the statement of last year, it gives us pleasure to note an 
advance of nearly fifty percent. We must, however, remember that when last year’s 
statement was submitted, the membership was in a rather depressed condition, on 
account of the very limited advantages then available, and we must confess to being 
rather disappointed at not being able to record fully two thousand members upon our 
books. 

We trust those who are already enjoying the many and splendid advantages of our 
building, will ever keep this work before them, and use all their influence to bring 
the young men and boys of our City into close connection with our work. 

A. R. WIGHTMAN, 
Chairman. 


PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT. 


The Committee beg to report that the year, although a broken one, has been 
full of enthusiasm, and ever since the z-door work of this Department opened, 
16th November, 1891, the building has been taxed to its utmost capacity by the 
crowds of young men in the Gymnasium Classes. The success of this work is in 
large measure due to our Physical Director, Mr. Ball, who, it is proper here to say, 
has won, and holds, the entire confidence of the Committee and the young men. 
He has managed and met with rare tact the various difficulties arising, and, being a 
thorough master of his business, has filled the bill in every respect, and the Associa- 
tion is certainly to be congratulated in having the Physical work under his charge, 
for in him they have a man who, while to his utmost endeavouring to help the young 
men physically, yet follows up his work by prayer, and a desire frst and dest to 
benefit them spiritually. He has been assisted by Mr. Corbett, as also by the 
Class Leaders, to whom great credit is due. Mr. Ball’s figures give some indication 
of the amount of work put through in this Department. 

Classes have been held on every day of the week, and twice or three times on 
Mondays, Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays. Upto Ist May, 465 young menand 
225 boys (total of 690) have taken the medical examination, most of them have also 
taken their ‘‘ manual,” giving the result of examination and prescription of special 
exercise suitable to their defects and requirements. To quote Mr. Ball’s report to the 
Committee: ‘* The'members have acted like gentlemen, a large number have been 
faithful to their work, and the absence of the few whose enthusiasm died out was 
hardly noticeable in the classes.” 


22 


The regulation uniform has been adopted by about half the members, and has _ 
met with general approval. q a 
The Bowling Alleys were not ready until March 21st, 1892. They are much | 
used and much appreciated : a small charge is made which suffices to pay the « pin 1 
boys,”’ and will leave something over for repairs and supplies. | 
The Gymnasium Apparatus has given every satisfaction, and, considering them 
immense amount of work it has had to do, has stood well and is now in good shape, 
The Plunge Bath is one of the Institutions of the Department, and literally 4 
crowded to overflowing. P 
The Lockers are satisfactory, but more are required, and the difficulty is going — 

to be to provide space for them. 515 out of the total of 604 Lockers have already q 
been taken. | 
The Out-door Work suffers from the disadvantage of not ownzng suitable r 
grounds, the provision of which is one of the pressing needs of the Association work, 
Last summer the Lacrosse Club practised in the M. A. A. Grounds. . 
Association Football Club played 5 games, won 4, and tied 1, and in the winter q 

the Snow Shoe Club kept up their usual “ tramps ’’ with a moderate attendance only, — 
Your Committee failed to obtain the use of the ‘“‘M. A. A. Grounds” for 4 
this summer, and are endeavoring to secure another suitable place for practice. This 
question will be an increasingly difficult one every year, and should be tackled in the 
immediate future by the Association, and grounds of their own on the River front, 
if possible, speedily secured. A ‘‘ Baseball Club” has also been organized, anal 
hopes to give a good account of itself during the season. | 
Dr. Gulick visited us in February and had intggesting ‘‘talks’’ with the 

‘* Classes.” 
A number of “ Exhibitions” by the Young Men’s and Junior Classes havell 
been ae from time to time, and many visitors highly delighted. a 
“ Confidential” talk was given to the young men by Mr. Ball, on April 22nd, 

with pslucat results. e 
D. W. ROSS, q 

Chairman Physical Department. . a

ROOM AND LIBRARY. 

Your Committee beg to report : it 
That the year has been a busy one. Their first work was to unpack, assort, and 
cull the books from the old library. Realizing the importance of their reading 
matter to the Junior Department, the members gave much time to the selection of 
boys’ books, and were able, after months of labor, to see on the shelves, arranged | 
and catalogued, about 800 volumes of the best books of travel, adventure, biography, - 
history, fiction and science. That these are interesting may be seen from the very 
large circulation—so large that the Committee has had to restrain it. Of the 336 
members of the Junior Department 260 are readers, and during the three months they 
circulation has been 1,846. r 
How to provide the necessary books for the hundreds of -junior: members on the 
appropriations which the Finance Committee was able to make has been a mos 
serious question. It remains so. The members of the Committee decided to mz ce 


23 


4 temporary arrangement and catalogue this part of the library, to draw on next year’s 
appropriations, and obtain the services of alibrarian. These have been accomplished. 
Some 200 volumes have been purchased, the latest and best in the different depart- 
ments of literature, a manuscript catalogue has been prepared, and the whole placed 
in the charge of a young fellow whose services have been prompt, gentlemanly, and 
efficient. So far the immediate wants have been met ; but what of the hundreds and 
thousands of new members in the future? 3,000 volumes are absolutely essential to 
the proper working of this new field ; and when it is remembered that most of our 
readers are dependent upon this source of reading matter, and will be greatly influenced 
by it, your Committee hope that special means may be obtained during the coming 
year for meeting this great and growing need.

F. W. KELLEY, 
Chairman. 


EVENING EDUCATIONAL CLASSES. 
The classes opened November gth, and a high average attendance was main- 
tained in all branches of study until the closing evening, which took place in April. 
Several new features were added this season, viz., the Chautauqua Literary and 


Scientific Circle, and the Elocution Class. 
The Orchestra have only now got well to work, and no definite report can be 


made.

SUNDAY MORNING CLASS. 


The Sunday morning class has been continued for another year and with good 
results. The early hour of meeting prevents its being largely attended, but those 
who have come have been able to realize, “ But they that wait upon the Lord shall 
renew their strength, they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run and 
not be weary, and they shall walk and not faint.” 


24 


During the spring it was deemed wise to change from a Bible Class to a Worker’s 
Prayer Service, at which the various Committees of the Association have been remem- 
bered before the throne of grace. The average attendance has been 20. 


YOUNG MEN’S MEETING. 


The past year has been one of varied experience in the history of the 
Saturday Night Meeting. 

Owing to the difficulties attendant on our removing from the old building, until 
we finally settled down in our present beautiful Meeting room, we have to report 60 
as the average attendance for the year. ; 

We find the card with the topics for each quarter very useful, as it enables 
members to look up the subject and come prepared to take part intelligently. 

The Committee, with the Chairman for the evening, come together for a few 
minutes before the Meeting, to plead for a special blessing on the work, and for the 
Holy Spirit’s guidance and direction. 7 

It is very pleasing to see how many young men are ready to take part either by 
testimony, exhortation or prayer, the interest during the whole time being well 
sustained. Just before the close of the Meeting an earnest invitation is extended by 
the Chairman for any who feel their need of a Saviour, or want counsel and help in 
the Christian life, to remain for conference and prayer. Almost every evening some 
respond to the appeal, and many good results have followed this personal contact. 
For after all, it is only when we live zz Christ and for Christ, that we are enabled to 
point ¢o Christ as the “all in all of every believer.” 

We would draw attention to the large field there is for work among the Associate 
Members. Large numbers of young men are being attracted to the different 
educational and physical classes, whom it is our duty to win for Christ. 

If each active member would consecrate himself to the bringing in of one of those 
young men into the fold, what a blessing would descend, not only on our work, but 
on ourselves, strengthening us to ‘‘ take courage and go forward,” in the work which 
He has given us to do. | 

J. M. CAMPBELL, 


Chairman. 


INVITATION. 


This Committeee has during the past year distributed 25,000 invitations. Our 
work consists of supplying the ‘‘ Take One” boxes at the Hotels and Railway 
stations, with invitations to the various meetings and every information regarding the 
Association. This is attended with good results. After prayer, we go out to the 
street corners and Windsor Hotel at 7.30 on Saturday night to give invitations for the 
8 o’clock meeting, and on Sunday afternoon at 2.30 for the Evangelistic Bible Class 
held from 3 to 4. We also do personal work, calling at the homes of young men 
on our way to the meetings, many of whom have been reached in this way. 

Our work has not been in vain. It is impossible to give the correct number of 
strangers who have responded to our invitations; but we know that a large number 
have by this means been introduced to the Association and its privileges, and we trust 
to Christ. | 


- 


25 


A marked development has been noticed in the members of this Committee, 
several finding it necessary to resign in order to take up other forms of Christian 
work. In this way there is a continual outflow, so that new workers are constantly 
needed to fill the vacancies. This fact proves that the Association develops men. 
One of our members, Mr. McGrath, represented the Committee at the London Con- 
vention. He returned greatly blessed, and better equipped for the Master’s service. 
E, J, WILLIAMS, 

Chairman, 


EVANGELISTIC BIBLE CLASS. 


Your Committee are pleased to report, notwithstanding the peculiar dis- 
advantages of the year, an average attendance of over 67, the total being 3,507. In 
the early part of our year the class membership was considerably affected by the 
alterations then being made in the old building, but in September and October it 
recovered somewhat, the average for the two months being 78. 

The numbers fell again, however, during our occupancy of the Dorchester 
Street Store, where they gradually dwindled down until December, when the average 
was only 54, on one Sunday but 42 being present, the lowest record of the year. 
From the opening Sunday in our new home, January 3rd, the class steadily increased, 
until, in April, the average stood 74. 

433 letters were sent out by the Attendance Secretary during the year, 392 of 
-which were to absentees, and gI to members of different Church Bible Classes, which 
-were closed during July and August, inviting them to join with us for these months, 
this invitation being taken advantage of by many. Nochanges have been introduced 
into the management of the class, and, when what we have is put into full operation 
and given a proper chance, great things may be expected. 

Until the end of June we continued to completion our course of ‘‘ Lessons 
from Jewish History,” running from ‘*The Captivity in Babylon” to Malachi’s 
prophecies concerning ‘‘ Messiah’s Messengers.” 

For the last remaining meetings in the old building, of hallowed recollection, 
and, as an appropriate beginning in the new, our leader provided us, in September, 
with a well-chosen programme drawn from ‘‘ The Life and Work of Jesus Christ,” 
which we still continue to consider, resulting in the bringing of many to ‘the way, 
the truth, and the life,”” and emphasizing to our Christian members the responsibility 
of ‘‘living Christ,” and how they may continue His work amongst their fellows. 
The teaching is the crystallization of years of practical experience in dealing with young 
men, and for those seeking instruction in Christian work the principles and practice 
may here be found. Many have left us during the year to become teachers in the 
Sabbath Schools connected with their different Churches, and a partial list of such 
furnishes seventeen names. 

Our Sub-Committee for the visitation of the sick has rendered good service 
~whenever called upon, but has experienced considerable difficulty owing to the back- 
~wardness of those who are unwell in reporting the fact to the Committee. 

We are very much indebted to Mr. W. T. Walmsley, our organist, and to Mr. 
W. A. Coates, who so kindly conducted the monthly practice of new hymns, for 


‘their faithful attentions throughout the entire year. 
W. J. WRIGHT, 


Chairman.

EMPLOYMENT. 4 

From May Ist, 1891, to April 30th, 1892, there have been 433 applications for 
employment accepted by the Committee, and of the number we have been — 
successful in eeChEDS employment for 103; this is an improvement of 24 on the 
previous year’s work. To the merchants of the city who have patronized our bureay — 
we return grateful thanks. It will give us pleasure to continue supplying them with ; 
help of any kind. We have always a large number of applications on file, and are — 
ready to supply firms with Clerks, Bookkeepers, Mechanics, Storemen, Gardeners, ; 
Coachmen, Xc., &c. D. W. CORBETT

We have now forty-five members contributing in sums from two cents to fity. 
cents weekly to the extension work ; which has for its object the extension of the 
work of the Young Men’s Christian Associations in this and other lands. The mona | 
collected has been apportioned to the following :— | 
Ist. In the partial support of Mr. David McConaughy in his work among the | 4 
young men of India, of whom there are fifty millions. 4 
2nd. In the work of the Provincial Committee, who have the supervision of the d 
extension of the work in Ontario and Quebec. 4 
3rd. The International Committee, who have the supervision of the work in the a 
United States and Canada. , 
4th. In the work of the Association Training School at Springfield, Mass. , whelll q 

so many men are being prepared for the work of the General Secretaryship. ‘ 3 
’ A pleasing part of our report in the year that has closed is the fact that so na 
members in the Junior Department are contributing. 
The thanks of the Committee are due to Mr. J. G. Darling for his faithful ; 
services as Secretary.

WM. SLOAN, Chairman. 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


It is almost impossible to give in detail the report of the whole year’s work, as 
that portion of it from May last till we entered into this building was somewhat 
disconnected and irregular. 

We desire to thank the Directors for the generous way in which they have 
equipped our rooms and given us every necessary means of carrying on the work, 
and making our Boys’ rooms the finest on this continent, and we can assure them 
that it has been money well laid out. 

During the year some of our members have joined their respective Churches, 
and we feel confident that they will become useful members in them. Several others 
who are over sixteen are being transferred to take their places on the Senior Com- 
mittees, and we trust that they may use their training to good advantage there. 

In consequence of a number of counter-attractions on the night of our Céte St. 
Antoine Meeting, and the large falling off in the attendance, it was thought 
advisable to discontinue it till the coming Fall, when we hope to resume it. A 
number of the boys come to our meeting here, and we are not losing our hold 
on them altogether. 

Our Committees have consisted of the following, viz., Religious, Invitation, 
Athletic, Social and Reception, and Bank, and have been catried on by 56 of the 
boys. 


RELIGIOUS WORK.

Two mass meetings were held, and were attended by 253 and 301 boys, from 
which we received splendid results and which we intend continuing quarterly. 

The number of inquirers since January was 89. Owing to this large number, it 
has been impossible to follow them all up, but, as we have their names and addresses, 
we hope to reach a number of them. Many of these have come out as followers of 
Christ, and are now doing good service for Him among the other boys. Three 
Training Classes have been carried on, attended by 25 boys, and from these we are 
seeing good fruit. A Monthly Prayer Meeting has been held to offer special prayer 
for our work, and we feel that this has brought upon us a great blessing. 

This Department was represented at the London, Ont., Convention by Mr. J. E. 
Millen, who read a paper on our work.

at an early date for the members, their parents, and friends,

ATHLETIC, it 
a 

This has been the best year in this line we have everhad. Our Snow-shoe Club 
numbered 93, and held weekly tramps’and football.matches at the Club House; 3 the 
latter took the form of a series of 11 matches between 8 teams, for a trophy in the 


shape of a pennant. The Gymnasium Classes have also been well attended. . of

The large difference between the withdrawals and deposits is, we think, account. ; 
able to the fact of the older boys, who are passing from us, closing their accounts. _ 

Our report would be incomplete without mentioning our Secretary, Mr. Corbett, 
upon whom the heaviest part of the work has fallen, and the faithful way he has 
rendered this service to the Lord. We feel he realizes he has been amply repaid 
for it by the results he has seen in the boys, and the blessing that has come to his 
own life. “ 

We wish to deknalodie God’s guiding hand in all we have been able to do, 
and the faithful way in which our Executive and Committeemen have done their 
respective work, and we look forward to the coming year with bright prospects for 


better work. ’ 4 
R. L. CHARLTON, =

RECEPTION COMMITTEE. 


Owing to the removal to the New Building, this Committee did not meet as in 
previous years, and the work, therefore, until December, was only partially done. 
During the opening week of the Building, and until January 14th, the number of 
visitors was so very large it was impossible to keep any record. The Committee 
Meetings since December have been 5, with an average attendance of 9, and the 
practical work has been done by 174 men during 88 evenings, an average of 2 each 
night : hours of duty 7.30 till Io. q 

During the month of April we have had one member on duty on Saturda ' 
afternoons from 3 o’clock till 5.30, and hope to continue this during the coming yea 5, 
it being much required. . a 


{ 


29 


The rooms are invariably closed with prayer, and the attendance at these 
devotional meetings has been very largely increased during the months of March and 
April; as these meetings give a good opportunity of speaking to young men as to their 
personal salvation, we hope all earnest workers of the Association will give us their 
presence on these occasions. Inviting strangers and members to the Saturday 
evening and Sunday afternoon meetings has been vigorously carried out. 2,500 
young men visit the rooms from Monday to Saturday; a daily average of 392 (this 
is exclusive of boys or of attendance at any meetings held in the Assembly Hall). 
148 is the average attendance of young men on Sundays (exclusive of the evening 
meetings held in April and May). During the coming year we hope, with the many 
advantages of the New Building, to be able to present a record of more practical 
work done. 

GEORGE W. JONES, 


Chatrman.
